summaries.example: Imagine Maya chooses to help clean up after a game. No one forces her, and helping fits what she wants to do. A compatibilist may say her choice can still be free even if her earlier experiences and the laws of nature helped cause it. The important question is whether she acted from her own wishes and reasons, rather than being pushed or controlled by someone else.
summaries.summary: Compatibilism is the claim that free will and causal determinism can fit together. Determinism says that the laws of nature and the distant past fix what happens. This can seem to threaten freedom: perhaps no one could have done otherwise, and perhaps actions began in causes outside the person. Incompatibilists say this threatens free will or moral responsibility. Compatibilists reply in several ways. Some defend a version of the ability to do otherwise. Others say the freedom needed for responsibility is not mainly about having alternate paths, but about acting from one’s own desires, values, or reasons. Some focus on whether a person’s action comes from a suitable part of the person’s psychology; others focus on being responsive to reasons or on our social responses such as resentment, guilt, and indignation. The entry presents these as different approaches, not one single compatibilist answer.
key_ideas: The free-will question asks how choice and responsibility fit with the causes of events.
Some philosophers think determinism means no one could have done anything else.
Others think freedom is mainly acting from one’s own wishes, values, or reasons without being forced.
Compatibilists disagree with one another about whether freedom needs different possible choices or a special kind of inner source.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps us ask what it means to choose, control an action, and deserve praise or blame. It also shows why philosophers can agree that people make choices while disagreeing about what makes those choices free. Understanding the disagreement can make everyday ideas about excuses, pressure, intentions, and responsibility more careful.

important_terms.definition: The view that free will can exist even if every event has causes that reach back through nature and the past.
The idea that everything that happens follows from the laws of nature and the way the world was before.
The ability to guide an action and be the person whose action it is.
Being responsible for what you do, so that praise or blame may make sense.
The idea that a person could have chosen a different action at the time of choosing.

questions_to_think_about: Is a choice free if nobody forces you, even if your wishes have causes?
Does being able to do something differently matter for being responsible?
How is choosing to help different from a body event, such as a heartbeat?
What might make a wish feel like your own?

summaries.example: Suppose Jordan decides to volunteer rather than study alone. In the actual situation, Jordan acts from reasons and values he understands. A hidden controller would have interfered if Jordan began to choose differently, so Jordan could not have avoided volunteering. Some compatibilists argue that Jordan may still be responsible because the controller never acted and Jordan’s own reasons-responsive decision process produced the action. Critics reply that the hidden setup may show that having the right inner process is not enough: the history that produced it may matter too.
summaries.summary: Compatibilism addresses the apparent conflict between free will and causal determinism. If determinism is true, the past and the laws of nature entail the future. This seems to threaten free will in two distinct ways. First, an agent may lack alternative possibilities: at the moment of action, she could not have done otherwise. Second, the agent may fail to be an ultimate source, because the sufficient conditions for her action existed before she existed. These concerns support two incompatibilist arguments. Compatibilists have replied that the relevant ability may be understood more modestly, that arguments from fixed facts to fixed actions may misuse ideas such as powerlessness, or that alternative possibilities are not required for responsibility. Frankfurt’s cases are designed to separate responsibility from the ability to do otherwise, although their interpretation remains contested. Other compatibilists analyze freedom through a match between effective desires and higher-order attitudes, through the ability to recognize and act on reasons, or through the interpersonal practices and reactive attitudes involved in holding people responsible. The entry emphasizes that compatibilism is a family of theories with different answers to the alternative-possibilities and sourcehood challenges.
key_ideas: The main challenge has two parts: determinism may remove alternative possibilities, and it may make agents seem less than ultimate sources of their actions.
The Classical Incompatibilist Argument moves from the thought that free action requires doing otherwise to the conclusion that determinism rules out free action.
The Source Incompatibilist Argument instead claims that free action requires the agent to be an ultimate source.
Compatibilists respond by rejecting one or more premises, by redefining the relevant ability, or by grounding freedom in guidance control rather than regulative control.
Frankfurt-style cases challenge the claim that moral responsibility always requires the ability to do otherwise, though the success of those cases remains disputed.
Contemporary approaches include hierarchical desires, acting for reasons, responsiveness to reasons, and interpersonal reactive attitudes.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue affects how we understand agency, deliberation, praise, blame, excuse, and responsibility. It also clarifies a major philosophical distinction: freedom to do otherwise is not obviously the same as control over the action actually performed. The debate asks whether a person’s psychological organization and responsiveness to reasons can ground responsibility, or whether responsibility requires a deeper kind of origin that determinism cannot provide.

important_terms.definition: The thesis that free will, and often the moral responsibility associated with it, is compatible with causal determinism.
The thesis that, given the laws of nature and the complete past, every event follows inevitably.
Control involving the ability to bring about an action and also to refrain from bringing it about; often linked to doing otherwise.
Control shown when an action issues from the agent’s own functioning decision process, even if alternatives were unavailable.
The idea that an agent must be the deepest origin of an action, rather than an outcome of sufficient conditions independent of the agent.
The principle that moral responsibility requires the ability to do otherwise.
A line of argument claiming that if no one controls the past, laws, or their entailments, no one controls the future consequences.
A theory that explains freedom through a suitable sensitivity of an agent’s decision process to reasons in relevant possible situations.

questions_to_think_about: Does moral responsibility require genuine alternatives, or is actual control enough?
Can an agent be a source of an action if the agent’s motives have deterministic causes?
Does a counterfactual ability count if changing the action would require a different past or different laws?
Do manipulation cases differ in a philosophically important way from ordinary deterministic histories?
Can social reactions such as resentment and guilt help explain responsibility, or do they presuppose it?

summaries.example: Imagine Leo is deciding whether to tell a friend the truth. He is not threatened or forced. He thinks about trust, remembers what happened, and tells the truth because he judges that it is the right thing. A compatibilist might say Leo acts freely because the action comes from his own reasons and decision-making, even if his character and past experiences helped cause his choice. An incompatibilist might answer that if those causes fixed the choice, Leo could not really have chosen otherwise.
summaries.summary: Compatibilism is the view that free will and causal determinism are not necessarily enemies. Determinism says that the laws of nature and the earlier state of the world fix what happens later. This creates a challenge because free choice is often understood as having alternatives: if only one future is possible, perhaps no one could have done otherwise. A different challenge says that free action must originate in the agent. If an action is guaranteed by conditions reaching back before the agent existed, the agent may not be its ultimate source. Incompatibilists use these ideas to argue that determinism rules out freedom or responsibility. Compatibilists answer in different ways. Some defend a meaningful understanding of alternative possibilities; others say that responsibility does not require alternatives and instead depends on guidance control. On these views, what matters may be that the action comes from the agent’s own desires, higher-order commitments, or reasons-responsive abilities. Strawson’s approach gives special importance to interpersonal practices and reactive attitudes such as resentment, guilt, and indignation. The entry presents an ongoing debate among several compatibilist theories.
key_ideas: Determinism appears to threaten freedom because it seems to leave only one possible future.
A second threat concerns sourcehood: if an action is guaranteed by conditions long before the agent acts, the agent may not seem to be its ultimate source.
Some compatibilists defend the idea that determinism does not remove every meaningful sense of doing otherwise.
Other compatibilists argue that responsibility needs guidance control, not necessarily regulative control.
Frankfurt’s examples question whether someone must have been able to do otherwise to be responsible, but philosophers continue to debate them.
Strawson-inspired views connect responsibility with the interpersonal attitudes and practices through which people respond to one another.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question matters whenever we decide whether someone chose, was forced, deserves praise, or deserves blame. It separates several ideas that are often blended together: having options, acting without outside pressure, controlling an action, and being the source of one’s motives. Studying compatibilism also shows how one philosophical problem can lead to different theories rather than a single agreed solution.

important_terms.definition: The position that free will is possible even if causal determinism is true.
The view that the past and the laws of nature together determine every later event.
Possible actions that an agent could select instead of the action actually performed.
The idea that a person is responsible only if she could have acted differently.
Being the origin of an action in a way that is not completely explained by conditions outside the agent.
The ability to control what happens by being able to perform an action or refrain from it.
Control shown when an action comes from the agent’s own reasons-guided process.
Emotional and interpersonal responses, such as resentment, guilt, or indignation, connected with holding people responsible.

questions_to_think_about: Is acting according to your own wishes enough for freedom?
Could someone be responsible for an action if a hidden condition guaranteed that action?
What is the difference between being caused to act and being forced to act?
Are reasons-responsive choices free even when the agent’s character has a causal history?
What do our reactions to wrongdoing reveal about moral responsibility?
